body.content: DRAFT: Consider a hypothetical variant of the problem where the target sum is 144 (mean 48, even). All neighbourhood methods yield 46,48,50. Now consider sum 150 (mean 50, even) → 48,50,52. The mean-principle methods generalize cleanly. But consider sum 141 (mean 47, odd). SRC_003's mechanism produces 45,47,49 — these are consecutive odd, not even. SRC_002's counterexample-first would reject all triples. SRC_001's mechanism notes 47 is odd and the triple is not even. The question: does any neighbourhood artifact have a countercondition that fires for 'mean is odd' specifically? Checking: SRC_001 says 'if 138 were not divisible by 3' — 141 IS divisible by 3, so this doesn't fire. SRC_003 says 'if not required to be even' — but the problem DOES require even. SRC_002 says 'if even constraint removed' — it isn't removed. SRC_004 says 'if common difference not 2' — it is 2. SRC_005 says 'if another triple also summed to 138' — uniqueness isn't the issue. So NONE of the neighbourhood counterconditions fire for the mean-is-odd case, yet the problem has no solution. This is a coverage gap.
body.possible_next_move: Construct simulation with S in {138, 141, 144, 147, 150} and check which artifacts' counterconditions fire.
body.unfinished: Need to determine whether the isolated artifact 0b13382ebfe2 has a countercondition that covers this gap.
body.why_keep_this: The mean-is-odd case exposes a coverage gap in neighbourhood counterconditions — if the isolated artifact covers it, that would support a 'complements' relation; if it also misses it, that supports 'reduces to'.
